spec.title: Two controls, one query, zero screenshots
spec.intro:
Module 01 proved one laptop's encryption claim by querying one machine. This lab is the
same discipline at cloud scale: the truth no longer sits in a file you can walk to — it
sits in the cloud's four parts, reachable only as data. You are asked to produce one
reproducible evidence report covering two controls — an encryption control (a STATE
question, answered by a posture-service finding) and an access control (an EVENT
question, answered by the audit log) — plus one SQL-derived risk metric, and to make the
whole thing re-runnable so it can later go on a monitoring schedule. The terminal is a
fidelity-pinned simulation of the lab box; the SQL console beside it is real SQLite
running in your browser, querying the evidence table your own setup run produces. One
honest boundary: `labs/happy-path.sh` is the repo's CI proof for this lab — it uses bash
constructs beyond this simulation's taught subset, so read it with `cat` here and run it
on a real machine.

tasks.instruction:
Stand in `~/lab07` and run `bash labs/setup.sh` — it stands in for the authenticated
pulls you would make against a real cloud's posture service and audit log, and writes
three fixtures into `fixtures/`. Then open `fixtures/posture-findings.json` with
`cat` and read it as data: one finding per resource, each a verdict from the cloud
part whose whole job is judgment.

hints.nudge: Collection first, evaluation second. The setup script IS the collection step — run it from `~/lab07`, then read what it pulled with the program that emits files.

hints.concept: §4.1 — the control plane is data, not a dashboard: ask for the record, not the picture

hints.reveal: bash labs/setup.sh — then read the pull: cat fixtures/posture-findings.json

tasks.explain:
You just did what a console screenshot can never do: pulled the posture service's
judgment as rows you can keep, diff, and count. Each line is a structured verdict —
resource, control, status — and the rest of this lab never reads anything else.

tasks.instruction:
Evaluate the encryption control for the in-scope resource: *"the bucket holding our
audit logs is encrypted at rest."* That is a state question, so the answer lives in
the posture finding. Pull the `audit-logs` finding line — whole and verbatim — into
`~/lab07/encryption-verdict.json` using `grep`, and read the verdict from its
`status` field. The evidence file must be produced by querying the record, not by
retyping what you saw.

hints.nudge: Which program keeps only matching lines? Match on the resource id and redirect the keeper's output into the evidence file — the finding goes in whole, timestamp-free and re-pullable.

hints.concept: §4.2/§5.1 — state questions are answered by the posture service, and the evidence is the finding itself, kept verbatim

tasks.explain:
The verdict is PASS, and your evidence is the cloud's own record — not your memory of
a green shield icon. Provenance matters as much as content here: a hand-typed copy of
the same bytes would be testimony, not evidence. This is module 01's laptop-encryption
claim again, answered at scale by a posture row instead of a one-machine query.

tasks.instruction:
In 2–4 sentences: classify each control question — *"is the audit-logs bucket
encrypted?"* and *"was a privileged role granted outside business hours?"* — as state
or event, name the cloud part that answers each (four-part model), and explain why a
posture snapshot could never answer the second one. Close with one sentence on why
you did not open a console for any of this.

hints.nudge: Snapshots prove the present; logs prove the past. By the time you snapshot the config, the suspicious timing has been erased.

hints.concept: §4.2 — state vs. events, the two kinds of cloud truth; §4.7 — why a query beats an export

tasks.instruction:
Evaluate the access control: *"no privileged role was granted outside business
hours."* Open `fixtures/audit-events.json` with `cat`, then build a two-stage filter:
keep only privilege-granting events (`AttachUserPolicy`), pipe those into a second
`grep -E` that keeps only grants whose hour is outside the 09:00–18:00 UTC window,
and redirect the survivors into `~/lab07/access-violations.json`. The offending event
must be kept whole; the in-hours grant and the `GetObject` data-plane decoy must not
be in your evidence.

hints.nudge: Two filters, one pipe: the first keeps the privilege grants (which also drops the data-plane decoy), the second keeps the bad hours. Out-of-hours is hour < 9 or hour ≥ 18 — as a pattern on the timestamp, that is hours 00–08, 18–19, and 20–23 right after the `T`.

hints.concept: §4.4 — an audit-log event is just a typed row; the control is evaluated by filtering events, and control-plane grants are not data-plane reads

hints.reveal: cat fixtures/audit-events.json, then: grep AttachUserPolicy fixtures/audit-events.json | grep -E 'T(0[0-8]|1[89]|2[0-3]):' > access-violations.json

tasks.explain:
One violation: a 2 a.m. grant of AdministratorAccess to contractor-7 — a finding no
configuration snapshot could surface, because by snapshot time the grant is just
"contractor-7 has admin" with the timing erased. Your filter also had to *ignore* a
row: GetObject reads data without changing the control plane, so it is not evidence
for this claim. Keeping the offending event whole preserves actor and timestamp for
the auditor.

tasks.instruction:
Turn rows into the number an executive actually asked for. In the SQL console (real
SQLite, loaded from the same `evidence.csv` your setup wrote), write one query that
produces a per-control failure rate — not just a count: group the evidence rows by
`control` and compute failing, total, and a `fail_pct` rounded to one decimal. Then
hand-check it in the terminal: count the FAIL rows for one control with
`awk -F,` over `fixtures/evidence.csv` and confirm the query's numerator.

hints.nudge: A rate is a summary of filtered rows: `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts the failures portably, `COUNT(*)` counts the bucket, and `GROUP BY control` makes one row per control. Avoid `SUM(status = 'FAIL')` — it works on SQLite but is a type error on PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle.

hints.concept: §4.5 — SQL is the grammar of evidence: the metric is the query, and the query re-runs unchanged against next quarter's table

hints.reveal: SELECT control, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'FAIL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failing, COUNT(*) AS total, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'FAIL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS fail_pct FROM evidence GROUP BY control; — hand-check in the terminal: awk -F, '$1 == "encryption" && $2 == "FAIL" { f++ } END { print f }' fixtures/evidence.csv

tasks.explain:
access 50, encryption 33.3 — that result set IS the risk report: it came from the
control plane, it reconciles against a hand count, and it is the same SQL whether the
rows originated in AWS, Azure, or GCP. One rendering honesty note: this is the real
engine's output — SQLite's shell prints 50.0 where the JS bindings print 50; the
module's prettified §5.3 table is representative, not byte-canon.

tasks.instruction:
Make it re-runnable. Compose `~/lab07/control-evidence.sh` (with `nano`, or `cat` and
a heredoc) that re-derives the verdict block from the fixtures every run: the
encryption verdict from the posture finding, the violation count from the audit
events, and the FAIL-row counts per control from `evidence.csv`. Then `chmod +x` it
and run `./control-evidence.sh` twice — the two outputs must be byte-for-byte
identical, and every number must be computed from the input files, never hard-coded.

verify.expect_stdout:
encryption: PASS
access violations: 1
encryption FAIL rows: 1 of 3
access FAIL rows: 1 of 2

hints.nudge: The script is the lines you already ran, saved — your t2 evaluation as an awk verdict, your t4 pipeline counted with `wc -l` inside `$( )`, and an awk FAIL-rows count per control. If any number is typed in as a literal, the check that re-runs your script in a clean environment will still pass — but your evidence stops being evidence.

hints.concept: §4.6 — deterministic evidence: separate collection (allowed to vary) from evaluation (a pure function of its input)

hints.reveal: nano control-evidence.sh with these five lines — #!/usr/bin/env bash · awk '/"resourceId": "audit-logs"/ && /"status": "PASS"/ { print "encryption: PASS" } /"resourceId": "audit-logs"/ && /"status": "FAIL"/ { print "encryption: FAIL" }' fixtures/posture-findings.json · echo "access violations: $(grep AttachUserPolicy fixtures/audit-events.json | grep -E 'T(0[0-8]|1[89]|2[0-3]):' | wc -l)" · awk -F, '$1 == "encryption" { t++ } $1 == "encryption" && $2 == "FAIL" { f++ } END { print "encryption FAIL rows: " f " of " t }' fixtures/evidence.csv · awk -F, '$1 == "access" { t++ } $1 == "access" && $2 == "FAIL" { f++ } END { print "access FAIL rows: " f " of " t }' fixtures/evidence.csv — then chmod +x control-evidence.sh and run ./control-evidence.sh twice

tasks.explain:
The reproducibility check just re-ran your script twice in a clean sub-environment
with the clock and entropy deliberately perturbed — and the outputs agreed, so the
determinism is a property of YOUR evaluation, not a fluke of the session. That is the
§4.6 contract: when this script's output changes on a monitoring schedule, the cloud
changed — not your code.

tasks.instruction:
In 2–3 sentences: explain why byte-identical output across runs is the precondition
for putting this check on a monitoring schedule, and what a `date`-stamped verdict
line would do to a drift alert. Name the discipline: which half of the work is
allowed to vary (collection) and which half must not (evaluation)?

hints.nudge: A monitoring alert you can't trust is worse than no alert: if the check's own output drifts, you cannot tell change in the world from noise in your code.

hints.concept: §4.6/§5.4 — same input, same verdict, every time

tasks.instruction:
Write the 4–6 sentence report an auditor would actually accept: map each verdict to
its control and name the cloud part its evidence came from (four-part model); state
each question's kind (state vs. event); say why your query-derived evidence is
stronger than an exported CSV or a screenshot; and describe how you would swap
`labs/setup.sh` for real authenticated pulls without changing one character of the
evaluation logic.

hints.nudge: The whole inversion in one move: don't describe the state and attach a picture — query the state and ship the code that did it. Collection swaps out; evaluation stays.

hints.concept: §3 — the four-part model; §4.7 — why a query beats an export

files.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Module 07 lab fixture generator (original lab asset).
# Usage: setup.sh [DEST_DIR]   (default ./fixtures)
# Produces three committed-style fixtures that stand in for real cloud control-plane pulls:
#   - posture-findings.json : one finding per resource (STATE; from the posture service)
#   - audit-events.json     : CloudTrail-shaped action records (EVENTS; from the audit log)
#   - evidence.csv          : one row per evaluated control instance (the evidence table for SQL)
# No cloud, no network. In the real lab these three pulls replace this script.
set -euo pipefail
DEST="${1:-./fixtures}"
mkdir -p "$DEST"

# STATE: posture-service findings for the encryption control. One PASS in scope, plus noise.
cat > "$DEST/posture-findings.json" <<'JSON'
[
  { "resourceId": "audit-logs",  "control": "encryption", "status": "PASS" },
  { "resourceId": "scratch-tmp", "control": "encryption", "status": "FAIL" },
  { "resourceId": "exports-q2",  "control": "encryption", "status": "PASS" }
]
JSON

# EVENTS: audit-log records. Two privilege grants; one is at 02:14 UTC (out of hours -> violation).
cat > "$DEST/audit-events.json" <<'JSON'
[
  { "eventTime": "2026-05-20T14:02:00Z", "eventName": "AttachUserPolicy", "actor": "alice",        "policy": "AdministratorAccess" },
  { "eventTime": "2026-05-20T02:14:00Z", "eventName": "AttachUserPolicy", "actor": "contractor-7", "policy": "AdministratorAccess" },
  { "eventTime": "2026-05-20T11:30:00Z", "eventName": "GetObject",        "actor": "alice",        "policy": "" }
]
JSON

# The evidence table: one row per evaluated control instance. SQL turns this into a risk metric.
cat > "$DEST/evidence.csv" <<'CSV'
control,status
encryption,PASS
encryption,FAIL
encryption,PASS
access,PASS
access,FAIL
CSV

echo "Module 07 fixtures written to $DEST/ (posture-findings.json, audit-events.json, evidence.csv)"
